2904.title: The platform’s own gates — run what CI will run
2904.content: Skill platform-gates: bun test passing is not the gates passing. What to run before you push, why the list is derived from the CI workflow rather than written down, and what a *:check failure is actually telling you to do. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . One command: . bun run cat gates # the fast set bun run cat gates --all # plus the jobs that need a browser bun run cat gates:list # see them without running them . Run it before you push, not after CI tells you.

2905.title: The CI workflow is the list
2905.content: This skill does not list the gates, because a written list drifts from CI and a stale list reads as authoritative, so nobody checks it. bun run cat gates derives the set from .github/workflows/code-quality-gates.yml at the moment you run it, so a gate added to CI is in your next local sweep. package.json is not the authority: many of its check: scripts appear in no workflow, and running all of them would fail you on things CI does not gate. The workflow’s own comments name the scripts it deliberately excludes, with a reason beside each (for example check:ci-health is a report about main, not a gate on your diff). Read the reasons there.

2906.title: bun test green is not the gates green
2906.content: The test suite, tsc --noEmit and the *:check gates fail independently. One cause can also fail two gates at once. Run the gate set, not just the tests.

2907.title: …and the gates green is not the PUBLISHED PAGE green
2907.content: Gates read sources. A defect that exists only in a renderer’s output — for example markup that Kramdown escapes because a Liquid whitespace-strip joined two attributes — passes every gate. | Gate coverage is bounded by what a gate can look at. Ask what the gates read, not how many there are. | When your change alters a rendered page, build the page. The site build is not in the fast loop. check:escaped-markup asks one narrow version of “the output is well-formed”, and only in docs-site.yml, where _site/ exists. If the real build will not run locally (the just-the-docs remote theme 403s through the agent proxy), stub the theme and build anyway; never substitute the thing under test. continual-progress §”A template is not a page” carries the discipline. | .

2908.title: …and a green gate is not a VERIFIED FACT
2908.content: A gate can see the artefact and still answer a different question from yours. A rule that lives only in prose has a compliance ceiling nobody measures. When you write a rule into prose, ask what would fail if somebody ignored it; if the answer is nothing, you have written a wish. The measurable form is a check, a schema field, or a test. A gate’s silence is bounded by its stated scope. check:stale-paths, for example, judges two shapes — an id adjacent to an arrow, and a numbered step under a path heading — and declines everything else. Prose that merely mentions a closed work item passes it while carrying the same defect. Likewise check:ci-health labels workflow files that produced no run unjudged, not green. Green over a narrow rule is worse than red, because red is examined; a gate that does not fire is indistinguishable from one that passed. Before quoting a tick as evidence: . What does this gate say it judges, and is my claim inside it? . Read the check’s own header — every one here states its scope and its declined cases — rather than inferring the scope from the fact that it ran.

2909.title: Fast versus full is job membership
2909.content: The split is read from the workflow at run time. | fast — the typescript job. No browser. This is the inner loop. | --all — adds the jobs that install Chromium. render:bpmn:check is there because bpmn-js renders through a browser, so it can pass locally only because a browser happened to be installed. | .

2910.title: Running “the gates that relate to my change” is not running the gates
2910.content: Pick the gate set by JOB MEMBERSHIP, never by which gates you judge relevant. bun run cat gates --all is the whole point of there being a command. A subset chosen by an author tests the author’s model of the change, and CI tests the change; they differ precisely where the bug is. gates --all takes minutes; a red CI run costs a push cycle. A verification names a tree . A verification names a TREE, not a branch. Anything edited after the run started is unverified, however green the run was. bun run cat gates reads the WORKING TREE, not the commit. An edit made while it runs leaves the change unverified, and can make the run report failures that were never in any commit. Nothing looks wrong when this happens: the run really passed, about a different tree from the one pushed. Run the gates after the last edit, not alongside it — if you edit while they run, the run is spent and needs doing again. A skill edit is the case most likely to produce this, because a skill body has two committed artefacts generated from it. A skill edit is three files: . | file | regenerate with | . | the body, skills/<pkg>/<name>.md | — you edit it | . | test/results/kg-qa/.../<name>.kg-qa.json | bun run cat kg:audit | . | docs/reference/skill-instructions/<name>.md | bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/gen-skill-docs.ts | . The kg-qa row is a derived QA result whose record is the commit-keyed entry the CI job qa-publish stores on the orphan qa-reports branch. While a committed copy exists, kg:audit:check compares against it, so regenerate it. bun run cat skill:register does all of it in one command. A minted term needs a gloss . termIri("X") MINTS a term, and a minted term needs a gloss. Adding a new @type or a new property in kg-export.ts is therefore a TWO-file change: the emitter, and schemas/content/vocabulary.ts (CLASS_GLOSSES for a type, PROPERTY_GLOSSES for a property). ns:check refuses the half done alone. This is a different gate from the export’s own undeclared-term report: one checks that the JSON-LD @context binds the term, the other checks that the namespace DEFINES it. Both must pass, and passing the first is not evidence about the second.

2911.title: What a *:check failure is telling you
2911.content: Most of these gates compare a committed artefact against what its generator would produce now. A red one almost never means “the artefact is wrong”. It means you changed an input and did not regenerate. So the fix is to run the generator and commit its output — never to hand-edit the artefact into agreement, which makes the next regeneration noisy and detaches the artefact from its source. QA gates have a different shape. A gate over the qa graph computes and judges: --check writes nothing, and fails only on a finding that is NEW against a baseline — the committed working copy, or --against <ref> on the qa-reports branch. A missing baseline is UNKNOWN, printed and never a pass, never a fail. The four judge states are ok (0), finding (1), unknown and error (2) — JUDGEMENT_EXIT in scripts/qa-results.ts. A red one of THOSE is a real finding your change introduced; regenerating does not clear it, fixing the subject does. Which gates have this shape is in each script’s own docblock. Each *:check script has a generator beside it under the same stem; bun run cat gates:list shows the check, and the script it checks is named in the check’s own output when it fails.

2912.title: …and a green gate set is not a CLEAN RUN
2912.content: bun run cat gates snapshots the tree before the first gate and after every one, so every gate can pass and the run still exit 1: . ✗ every gate passed, and the run is NOT clean — 1 gate(s) changed the tree. The gates after the mutation were handed the repaired tree, so their verdicts describe a state you have not committed. gate-tree-mutation (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) carries the two causes, the one command that tells them apart, and the question that settles the second: does the churning field describe the subject the artefact is about, or the run that produced it? Only the first is a reason to write.

2913.title: Three things this skill will not do for you
2913.content: It does not replace reading the failure. The runner names the failing command and the CI step it belongs to, so a local failure and a red PR are findable by the same string. Read what the gate printed. It does not tell you a gate is wrong. A gate whose purpose you cannot state gets “fixed” by being made to pass, which turns the check into decoration. Every gate in that workflow carries a comment saying what it catches; if you think one is wrong, that comment is what you are arguing with. It does not make --all optional before a push that touches a diagram. Anything under processes/ changes a rendered SVG, and the check for that is in the browser job.

2914.title: If bun run cat gates reports no gates
2914.content: It fails rather than exiting clean: an empty sweep that exits 0 is indistinguishable from a passing one. If you see that refusal, the workflow was renamed or restructured and the reader needs fixing — not the gate list.

2915.title: Related
2915.content: |   |   | . | .github/workflows/code-quality-gates.yml | the authority, with a comment per gate saying what it catches | . | scripts/gates.ts | the reader, and the vacuity guard | . | continual-progress | commit early, open the PR at the first commit — this is the step before the push | . | prepare-merge (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) | the pre-merge recipe, which runs these plus content-type gates | . | ci-health | whether the workflows themselves are working — a different question | . | gate-tree-mutation (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) | reading NOT clean — a green gate set over a tree a gate repaired | .

2916.title: platform-gates (skill)
2916.content: The skill platform-gates as its source file cat-harness/skills/process/process-core/platform-gates.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

2917.title: Remote-mount a harness
2917.content: Skill remote-mount: Bring a harness, and every layer it depends on, into a checkout that does not hold it, from another repository at a pinned commit, as declared directories with a lock: a source.remote entry in the downstream’s root index.config.json (legacy: remoteMounts on its declaration) and mountDefaults on the harness. Covers when to mount and when to subscribe instead, why there are no submodules and no .deps/, the transitive closure through needs and gitlinks, overrides by id, the lock, and the three states. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . How a downstream folio gets the layers it is built on: . | no git submodules, ever; | no .deps/, because a dot directory collides with GitHub’s conventions and with this repository’s own dot-prefix guard; | a remote mount is a declared directory with a remote source, pinned to a full 40-character SHA; | the defaults live in the harness’s own declaration, so a downstream never restates the paths; | a downstream may override them by id, never by path; | mounts are resolved transitively across the dependency closure; | code arrives through the mounted code directories. | . |   | where | . | the process | mount-dependency.bpmn; the per-subgraph view is the remote and npm flows of mount-subgraph.bpmn | . | the schema | cat-harness/schemas/kg/remote-mount.ts, plus the remote, npm and hydrated members of SubgraphSource (schemas/kg/subgraph-source.ts); the per-pin index package is subgraphIndexPackage in schemas/kg/subgraph-manifest.ts | . | the tool | bun run cat mount:remote (--plan to resolve without writing), and bun run cat mount:remote:check (offline) | . | the entry point | bun run cat state:mount, which the session-start hook already runs | .

2918.title: Mount, subscribe or associate: choose first
2918.content: | you want | relation | what arrives | . | to build on a harness: run its scripts, import its schemas, read its skills as your own | remote mount (source.remote in index.config.json) | the harness’s declared directories and those of everything it needs, at one pin | . | to read another graph and hold chosen parts of it | subscription (subscriptions): the kg-subscription skill | a snapshot of its declaration, then parts you materialise one at a time through the five gates | . | to know of a harness and link to it | association (associatedHarnesses): the associate-harness skill | nothing | . | to retrieve or distribute as a package | npm distribution (kg-retrieve-npm, source.npm): the npm-kg-distribution skill | an npm .tgz tarball (unhydrated source or hydrated view) | . The test is whether your code imports theirs. If it does, mount. If you only read their content, subscribe: a subscription gates every part through copyright and purpose, and a mount does not, because the code it brings is the platform you are built on.

2919.title: The two halves of the declaration
2919.content: The harness side goes in the harness’s own <name>.json and is written once by the harness’s owner: . "mountDefaults": { "path": "cat-harness", "directories": ["schemas", "scripts", "skills"] } . What arrives is what the declaration NAMES: the declaration itself, the chosen directories, and the instance-scoped files in its assets (its README and AGENTS.md). A file the declaration does not name, such as a platform.ts beside it, never arrives. Code the mounted graphs import has to sit in a declared directory. Both fields are optional, and each absence has a meaning: . | path absent means the layer’s home path (livesAt.path, else its directory in its own repository). | directories absent means every declared directory whose content is in the checkout. A branch, family or remote source is somebody’s state, not part of the harness. | . The downstream side goes in the checkout’s root index.config.json, as the source.remote of the layer it brings in. Which layers a checkout instantiates, where each comes from, and the fallback for a folio with no index are index-config’s rule. This skill covers only what a remote source means once it is declared: . { "name": "<harness>", "source": { "remote": { "repository": "<owner>/<repo>", "ref": "<40-character sha>", "overrides": { "cat-harness": { "directories": ["schemas", "skills"] }, "bootstrap": { "skip": true } } } } } . The fields are a remoteMounts entry without its harness, because the layer’s name is the harness (RemoteSourceSchema in schemas/kg/index-config.ts). A folio with no index still reads remoteMounts on its declaration. Declaring a mount in both places is an error: readDeclaredMounts throws and names both files. bun run cat index-config:migrate --write moves the entries across. Every tool that writes mounts writes through writeDeclaredMounts, into index.config.json, and none writes remoteMounts. overrides is keyed by layer name, then by directory id: . | path moves a layer. | directories replaces its default list. An id may be one the layer declares in its <name>.json or from within one of those directories (a "subgraph": true entry of skills/skills.json, such as voices); both are resolved at the pin through instanceDirectories, the resolver every on-disk reader uses. A nested id mounts its own path alone. An id declared in neither place is refused, not dropped, and the refusal says where it looked. The same holds for the harness’s own mountDefaults.directories. An id may also be a concern name, a code from code-lists/concern-group.json such as sdlc. It expands to every kind-first member the layer declares, such as sdlc/processes/ and sdlc/skills/, read from each grouping kind’s own declaration file at the pin. Each member is locked as <directory id>/<code>. A code that none of the layer’s kinds declares is refused like any other unknown id. | After a review of hydrated metadata, `mount:remote –choose [:] --directories a,b --tools x,y` writes the choice into `overrides.` (the choice, never the state), so a fresh clone replays it. It ends the review: that layer mounts as files, so its `hydrated` is dropped. The pin and consent do not move. | skip leaves it unmounted, and the lock records it as an answer. | tools names Tools this layer declares, by id, and mounts each one runnable: its definition, its implementation and their import closure. The next section but one says what that brings. | hydrated: true (here, or on the entry for its harness) mounts each chosen directory as one file: its published index.hydrated.jsonld at the pin, a hydrated source. Read what is there, then choose what to mount as files. No declaration is laid down, and needs is not followed. Where that file comes from is the next section. With no directories, a hydrated mount offers every top-level in-checkout subgraph and ignores mountDefaults.directories on purpose: that list chooses which FILES a downstream gets, and a hydrated mount is the step before choosing. Each top-level file already carries its nested subgraphs inline (hasSubgraph), so a nested one is named only when you want it on its own. | .

2920.title: Hydrated: the index files are published per pin, in a package
2920.content: A pin’s subgraph index files (index.jsonld, index.hydrated.jsonld under <docs>/subgraph/<HARNESS>/) are published per pin in a package, and a hydrated mount fetches them through the Tool its source names (the hydrated source’s tool, which is remote-mount unless it says otherwise). | Not committed in each repository. The files are builtAtPublish: they are computed over the checkout’s other layers, so no commit can hold them current, and a committed copy turns every re-pin’s check red. | Not generated at mount time. The downstream would need the whole index, kg-export and the framing toolchain to read one file of metadata, which is the cost a hydrated mount exists to avoid, and two downstreams could frame two different files for one pin. | . What that means in practice: . |   |   | . | the package | <harness>-subgraph-index@0.0.0-pin.<sha>: the index files at their published paths, and subgraph-index.json (folio-subgraph-index/v1) giving each file’s sha256 and the repository, pin and harness | . | where | assets of the GitHub release subgraph-index-<sha> in the layer’s repository, with the tarball’s folio-binary-release/v1 record beside it. Every name is computed (subgraphIndexPackage in schemas/kg/subgraph-manifest.ts) | . | who publishes | the subgraph-index-package Tool, run on every push to main by the reusable workflow layer-publish-subgraph-index.yml (the tools layer); a harness opts in with one uses: line | . | what a mount checks | the pin’s git tree first (a commit that does carry the file still works); otherwise the package: the tarball against its record (size, sha256), the manifest against the repository, pin and harness asked for, each file against its sha256, then the same schema and subgraph-IRI check a tree file gets | . | the lock | a directory that came from the package records the tarball’s URL and sha256 and the file’s path in it (package), so mount:lock fetches the same bytes and refuses any others | . No release for the pin is missing, and the detail says the package was looked for. A package that fails a check is missing; one that could not be fetched is could-not-determine. Neither is ever an empty mount. The record travels with the tarball, so its digest proves the transfer, not the publisher: who may publish is the repository’s write access, the same trust the git tree at the pin already rests on.

2921.title: Tools: choose by id, mount runnable
2921.content: The workflow: load the Tools’ metadata, review it, then materialise a chosen set. The first step is a hydrated mount of the declaring layer’s tools directory. Its index.hydrated.jsonld holds every Tool whole, and each Tool is its own tools/<id>/ subgraph. The last step is tools on that layer’s override: . "overrides": { "cat-harness": { "tools": ["bean-query", "bpmn-checklist", "agent-memory"] } } . Three rules govern this step: . | A Tool brings both halves. Its definition is <tools dir>/<id>/<id>.ts in the layer that declares it, by the folder convention in schemas/tools/tool-folders.ts. Its implementation is what its invoke names: . | inProcess.module, found in the declarer or in a layer whose needs names it (resolveImplementingPath’s rule; two holders is refused); | the script a bun run cat <key> command resolves to through the layers’ checkoutScripts. | . A bare runtime command (gh, beans) or manual brings no code. Both halves arrive with their import closure. A definition without its code is not a Tool you can run, and code without the modules it imports does not load: either way the checkout is half-working. | One closure walker. The closure is bootstrap-tools’ importClosure (scripts/check-closure.ts). check:tools-closure and the staging cone use the same walk. Do not write a second walker: two of them give two answers to “what does this code load”. | Directory granularity. The mount brings every declared directory the closure touches, whole. It takes the most specific declared directory (a nested one such as skills/voices mounts alone) and never a single file, so the lock schema is unchanged. A closure file in no declared directory, and an import that resolves to nothing, are refused with the file named. Neither is ever dropped. | . With tools named anywhere in a mount entry, each layer of that entry mounts the directories the closure touches, plus any its override names in directories. It does not mount its default list. A whole layer stays whole. A Tool id the layer does not declare at the pin is refused at plan time. tools together with hydrated is refused, because metadata brings no code. What it costs. A Tool folder is not a declared directory: tools/ is, and most definitions import its lib.ts. So a definition arrives with the whole tools directory, which holds every Tool’s definition. The cost that matters falls on the implementation side, which brings the directories its closure touches (in the tools layer, typically scripts and src). Without tools, the tools layer mounts every in-checkout directory it declares. The end-to-end check is the remote-mount test “load tools metadata, choose three Tools, materialise them” in the tools layer.

2922.title: Why the default path is the home path
2922.content: At its home path, a mounted layer keeps its position relative to its siblings. Two things then follow with no extra machinery: . | instanceRootsIn scans one level deep, so it finds every mounted sibling and needs resolves exactly as it does in the monorepo. | A relative import such as ../../cat-harness/schemas/… finds the file it names. | . Moving a layer by override is allowed, and the overlay still finds it through the lock (mountedInstanceRoots, mountScopeFor). The override is then responsible for any import that climbs out of the moved layer.

2923.title: The closure
2923.content: . | The harness’s declaration is read from the pinned tree, not from this checkout. | Each needs name is looked for in the same tree. | If it is not there, the planner looks for a gitlink at that tree’s root. A submodule entry is itself a pin, so a need on bootstrap resolves to litlfred/bootstrap at the gitlink’s SHA. The downstream gets the bytes and never a submodule. | A need the downstream already holds as a local layer is local: it is supplied by the checkout and never mounted over. | A need found nowhere is missing. It is never dropped. | .

2924.title: The lock, and the three states
2924.content: index.lock.json sits beside the downstream’s index.config.json and is committed. It is generated by mount:remote and never hand-edited, which is why it is a separate file rather than part of the index. Readers also accept the legacy name <name>.mount-lock.json, and both present is an error. It records: . | the pins it was written for; | for each layer: the repository, the SHA, how the pin was found (declared / same-tree / gitlink), the declaration’s digest, each directory’s tree digest, and declared layer assets (such as package.json); | what was not mounted, and why. | . The mounted bytes are not committed. With an index, each mount path is ignored by a generated block in the root .gitignore, written from the index (check:index-ignores is the gate). A path that block does not cover is reported as missing, never patched locally, because a local exclude is invisible to every other clone. In a folio with no index, a path its rules do not ignore goes into the worktree’s info/exclude. Mount path and route collisions. A mount with no path override lands at <name>/ in the downstream root, beside the downstream’s own directories, and its site routes sit beside the site-wide ones. To prevent collisions on disk and in route space: . | Reserved names: RESERVED_ROOT_AND_ROUTE_NAMES in schemas/kg/remote-mount.ts declares the one authoritative list of reserved root directories and site route names: ["skills", "tools", "docs", "assets", "glossary", "api", "payload", "branches/", "beans", "todos", "fsh-guts", "uploads", "test", "build", "_site", "_docs", "_kg"]. | Mount path check: checkMountPathCollisions (run during planning in mount:remote and by bun run cat check:mount-collisions) rejects any remote mount whose effective path (path or <name>/) collides with: . | a directory the downstream declares in its own configuration; | a reserved root or site route name; | another mount’s path. When a collision occurs, the error states how to fix it: “set path” (on the layer’s overrides.<name>.path in index.config.json or source.remote.overrides). | . | Route rules: . | Canonical: every visualiser is reachable at <base>/<harness>/<visualizer>/. Every generated link uses that form unless an alias is declared. | Alias: <base>/<visualizer>/ exists only when a declaration opts in via alias: true or alias: "<alias>" in its Visualisation declaration (coverage.visualiser). The site build refuses an alias that collides with another alias, a harness route, or a reserved site route, and names both claimants. | The route rule itself is in schema-management §”Where a viewer publishes”. | . | . Every layer ends in exactly one state: . | state | means | exit | . | mounted | on disk, hashing to the lock | 0 | . | unverified-approver | mounted, on consent no mountApprovers list checked | 0, reported apart | . | missing | not on disk, edited since mounting, not in the tree, refused, or the lock is for other pins | 1 | . | could-not-determine | the fetch failed, a declaration or lock is unreadable, or a layer is reached at two pins | 2 | . Could-not-determine outranks missing, and missing outranks mounted. A fetch that failed is never an empty layer. A fresh clone: the root’s cat bootstrap . A downstream root’s cat script is bun .github/cat.ts, not the bare runner. The runner (scripts/run-script.ts of the tools layer) is itself a mount, so on a fresh clone it is not on disk.github/cat.ts checks for it and, when it is missing, runs .github/mount-from-lock.sh (which fetches mount-from-lock.ts at the commit the lock pins for the tools layer and replays the lock, verifying every tree digest) before it hands over with the same arguments. So bun run cat <name> works from git clone with no mount step. It checks only that the runner is present, so after a re-pin run bash .github/mount-from-lock.sh by hand to replace the stale mounts. instantiate-harness.ts writes both files from the tools layer’s templates/root-bootstrap/ and sets the cat script. A root set up before that keeps a cat script that runs the bare runner until the two files are copied in. Re-pinning: from a checkout mounted from the lock . A re-pin is mount:remote --seed <name>=<owner/repo>@<sha> (it writes the pin and its consent into index.config.json), then mount:remote (it lays the bytes down and rewrites the lock). Do it in a checkout whose mounts match the lock: a fresh one, or one replayed by .github/mount-from-lock.sh. A mount with local edits is left untouched by the next mount, at its old commit, while the lock’s top-level pin moves, so CI would keep testing the old layer. --seed refuses while a mount it moves has such edits, and mount:check reports a layer entry behind its pin as missing. After the re-pin, check that the moved layer’s sha in index.lock.json is the new pin. A pin only moves forward (owner ruling, 2026-11-06, card “Pin target”, A). When layers pin different commits of a shared layer, align them forward, bottom-up: start at the lowest layer, and move each shared layer to the newest commit that any layer needs. Stop when every lock names one commit per layer. Never move a pin back to an older commit so that two layers agree. A re-pin is a cross-layer set (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). Pin together every layer the change needs, re-pinned to the current mains, and verify on a fresh mount (mount:remote --fresh). A layer can need another layer’s newer commit. For example, cat-harness#1100 removed routes that were listed by hand, because a content layer above it now derives them (builtOnHostSite). So cat-harness at 6dd3746 or later needs that content layer’s change, and the tools layer’s matching one, in the same re-pin. An asset that a layer commits must also match the tools recipe that generates it, such as cat-harness’s edit-links.js. A re-pin is its own PR (owner ruling, 2026-11-07: “keep repins on own PR so easier to stack dependencies”). A re-pin PR changes the pins and nothing else: index.config.json, index.lock.json, the generated uses: pins, and what regenerates from them. It carries no feature change, no workflow logic and no fix. | A feature that needs the new pins is stacked on the re-pin PR (below) rather than riding inside it. | A fix that the re-pin needs lands in the layer that owns it, and the re-pin then only moves the pin. | Counter-example: folio-assistant#2985 carried #2999 (the shared ci-setup move) and its own caches:viz gate line inside the re-pin. | The one exception: mutual dependence (owner ruling, 2026-11-07, card, about 08:43Z, “A. Allow the exception”). A re-pin may share a PR with a change only when neither can pass on its own. The PR body must say why. Example: a content layer re-pinned to cat-harness#1032 failed check:tools without its own PR’s library topic, and that PR alone declared the library topic twice against the old pin. A change that merely needs the new pins is not mutual: it stacks. | . A lower layer’s new gate must not break the next re-pin. A gate or check script added to a lower layer has passed a downstream dry run before it lands, so a re-pin moves pins and nothing else. When a re-pin nonetheless fails on a gate a lower layer just added, the fix goes into that layer, not into the re-pin (prepare-merge (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”A new gate in a lower layer must pass downstream”). Stacking across layers (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). Work that needs an unmerged PR in a lower layer does not wait for it. Develop against that PR’s branch laid over a fresh mount. A draft PR may pin the dependency PR’s full 40-hex head SHA so that its CI sees the change. A branch is never pinned, as for any pin. That draft is never marked ready or merged while it pins an unmerged commit: once the dependency lands, re-pin to its merge commit on main. That move goes forward, so “a pin only moves forward” holds throughout. The re-pin refreshes layer health (owner ruling, 2026-11-07, card “Layer health”, A). When a re-pin moves the tools layer, it regenerates the checkout’s layer health report at the new pins and publishes it. The health check fails a re-pin once the report is more than 26 hours old and the checker has moved. The tools layer implements it. The committer re-pins, locally, and CI only verifies. The person or agent who moves a pin does the whole re-pin in their own checkout: --seed, a fresh mount:remote, the regenerated agent surface (skill:commands, agent-memory, index:render), and the local checks. That same mount:remote then publishes the new lock’s layers cache ref (below) alongside the branch, with whatever credential pushes the branch. bun run cat layers:publish retries it, and --no-layers-publish skips it. CI never builds the ref when it exists: it fetches it and verifies it against the lock. Two writers are only fallbacks: . | the re-pin train, for layers nobody re-pinned; | main’s post-merge workflow, which rebuilds the ref for every push that changes index.lock.json. | . The layers cache: one fetch, every byte still verified . Replaying a lock fetches each pinned layer from its own repository. The layers cache is one git commit in the INDEX repository whose tree is the composed overlay a replay lays down: each locked directory at its mount path, each declaration and asset, and nothing an install, a state mount or a publish build wrote. | Ref: refs/cat/layers/<key>, where the key is the sha256 of the lock’s instances. refs/cat/layers/main moves with main’s lock. | Reader: mount:lock, and through it .github/mount-from-lock.sh, the session-start hook and every CI job, first tries ONE shallow fetch of the key’s ref, then of main. A layer whose copy verifies is laid down from it. A layer that does not verify, or a ref that is missing, is fetched from its own repository as before. --no-layers-cache (or CAT_LAYERS_CACHE=0) skips it, and CAT_LAYERS_URL points it at another remote. | Writer: the committer, through mount:remote or layers:publish. It refuses unless every mount reads current, then pushes the overlay. --main also moves main. --prune <n> keeps the newest n lock refs, main, and each --keep <key>, for example the lock of every open PR. | Gate: on an index-mode pull request that changes index.lock.json, the job layers-ref of the tools layer’s layer-pr-checks.yml runs layers:check --changed-from <base>. It only asks (git ls-remote) whether the new lock’s ref is at the repository, and fails when it is not. The build and the push stay on the re-pinner’s machine, never a runner (owner, 2026-11-08). A PR that leaves the lock alone owes nothing. | Shared fallback: an IG whose origin carries no refs/cat/layers/* can name a shared cache in .github/layers-url (one URL). The root bootstrap’s mount-from-lock.sh then sets CAT_LAYERS_URL to it. Only layers at the same pin hit; the rest are fetched as before. | . The lock stays the sole authority. The cache is untrusted. Every byte taken from it is checked against the lock: the declaration’s and each asset’s sha256, and each directory’s treeDigest. These are the same checks a fetched byte passes. So a stale main still serves every layer that did not move, and a tampered ref costs time, never correctness. Trust is unchanged: consent was checked when the lock was written, and the cache cannot add a layer the lock does not name. A replay that fails is reported loudly, not swallowed: a stale mount makes local checks pass falsely.

2925.title: A changed lock re-renders the agent surface
2925.content: A mount is not done when the bytes are on disk. A newly pinned layer can bring new skills, renamed skills and new agent-memory entries, but an agent does not read the layer: it reads what is generated from it. | surface | generated by | from | . | .claude/commands/<name>.md | skill:commands | every user_invocable skill in the mounted kg graphs | . | .claude/agent-memory/<agent>/MEMORY.md, .agents/skills/, .agents/rules/ | agent-memory | the memory directories the mounted layers declare | . So when a mount:remote run changes the lock, it runs both generators from the checkout root before it exits, and a generator that fails fails the run. A re-pin commit then carries the new layers and the surface rendered from them. --no-agent-surface opts out; --check, --plan and --staging never run it, since they change no lock a commit would carry. The list lives in one place, AGENT_SURFACE_GENERATORS in cat-harness-tools/scripts/remote-mount.ts. A new generator of something an agent reads (a rule file, a settings hook) is added there, not to a checklist: a step a person has to remember is the step that gets skipped. The process step is Task_RenderAgentSurface in mount-dependency.bpmn, between writing the lock and checking against it.

2926.title: Trust: what lets a mount proceed (H8)
2926.content: A real mount needs a person’s consent for that pin (trust.consent); a --staging mount needs none. schemas/kg/mount-trust.ts has the rules. Four things to know: . | The lock records the basis for each layer: staging, or consent with who and when. mount:remote:check re-runs the trust check against the current declaration, so consent withdrawn later reads refused. | A gitlink needs consent of its own. A layer reached through a gitlink is another repository at another commit. Give its consent on overrides.<name>.trust, for the gitlink’s SHA. | Who may consent. Declare mountApprovers and a consent.by not on the list is refused. Without the list, mounts report unverified-approver: exit 0, but never shown as clean. A checkout whose mounts index.config.json lists declares the list there, as its top-level mountApprovers; declaring it on the layer declaration as well is an error. | A refused mount is not current. Its old bytes stay on disk (an agent does not delete them). The lock records them under unmounted as leftOnDisk, and the check reports them as not mounted. | . Standing consent: a site keeps itself on an upstream branch . Pins stay per site. A site may declare, on one layer’s trust.standing, that a named person consents to following a branch — {follows: "main", consentBy, consentAt, require?: "green"}. The repin tool (cat-harness-tools/scripts/repin-standing.ts, run by its standing-repin.yml workflow) then moves that pin to the branch’s newest (green) commit and writes trust.consent for the new pin, by that person and marked standing. The mount accepts it only while the same rule is still declared: withdraw or edit it and those pins ask again. A pin moved by hand still asks again, rule or not.

2927.title: Publishing a remote-mounted downstream — provision gh-pages first
2927.content: A mount brings layers into a checkout; it provisions nothing on the downstream’s remote. A downstream that publishes a site needs a gh-pages branch before GitHub Pages can be switched on, exactly as a new repository does. The step is Task_ProvisionGhPages (“Provision gh-pages”) in the getting-started process (getting-started §5), with the semantics of A_Provision in bootstrap-tools’ render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn. Run bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts --provision (idempotent, never forced; without the flag it only reports unprovisioned and the exact command), then set Pages to “Deploy from a branch: gh-pages, / (root)”. A worked example is in repo-conversion §5.

2928.title: Never
2928.content: . | Never add a submodule to get a dependency, and never clone into .deps/. | Never pin a branch or an abbreviated SHA. The schema refuses both. | Never move a pin back. Align layers forward to the newest commit any of them needs (§”Re-pinning”). | Never edit a mounted directory and expect a re-mount to keep the edit, or to throw it away. A re-mount leaves edited bytes untouched and reports them as missing. Move the edit upstream, or delete the directory and re-mount. | Never mount over tracked files, or over a directory that no lock says this mount made. Both are refused. | Never read missing or could-not-determine as “that layer has nothing in it”. A layer that is not mounted is absent from every overlay. | .

2930.title: Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN
2930.content: Skill render-kg-to-cdn: Render a Knowledge Graph, or a list of its Subgraphs, for publication to a CDN at a publication root URL, and report a status and one message. The same step for a staging preview and for a release — only the root URL and the target differ. Names the target’s Tool, never its steps: GitHub Pages (gh-pages) is one Tool, and it carries its own subprocess. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . Render the content of a Knowledge Graph, or a list of its Subgraphs, for publication to a CDN at a given publication root URL, independent of staging or release, and report the status of the push with a message. GitHub Pages is one Tool for this general step. Drawn as render-kg-to-cdn.bpmn.

2931.title: Inputs and output
2931.content: | input | what | . | Knowledge Graph | a layer root — or a tree the caller has already rendered and verified | . | Subgraphs | optional: declared directory ids; absent means the whole graph | . | publication root URL | where the rendering is served | . | CDN target | which Tool performs the push — a Tool that satisfies: ["render-kg-to-cdn"] | . | output | what | . | status | pushed, not-pushed, or could-not-determine — a check that could not look is never pushed | . | message | one line, postable as it stands: what is live (a commit), where, and the QA result | .

2932.title: Staging and release are the same step
2932.content: A preview is this with a root under the release root; a release is this with the release root. What differs belongs to the caller: who may start it, what must be reviewed or verified first, what else lives on the same host and must survive the push. That is why feature-staging and docs-site-publish both call this process rather than restating it, and keep their own steps — the slug, the render log, restoring the open previews, the publication-manager alert — around the call.

2933.title: Name the Tool, not its steps
2933.content: The general process has one call activity, bound by the Tool: the activity names this skill, the Tool for the chosen target satisfies it, and the Tool lists its own subprocesses — the diagram of its steps (skills-and-tools, bpmn-processes). The general skill never lists them. | target | Tool | its subprocess | its message | . | GitHub Pages | gh-pages | bootstrap-tools processes/render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn | the commit merged onto gh-pages + the QA of what is staged and what is served | . A target may need provisioning before it accepts a push; the Tool’s subprocess owns that. For GitHub Pages a gh-pages branch has to exist before Pages can be switched on to serve it, so the gh-pages subprocess creates it first — the general step does not. Another CDN is another Tool with its own subprocess, and nothing here changes. A CDN in front of an origin is a layer, not a publication host (kg-to-portal): the publication root URL stays the origin’s canonical one even when a CDN serves it.

2934.title: What this is not
2934.content: Not the verification of what a build produced — that is publish-verification, and it runs before a caller hands its tree over. Not the decision to release — the content layer’s publication step and release-lifecycle. This step renders, pushes, and says whether the push landed.

2936.title: Sub-KG lifecycle — staged here, separated later
2936.content: Skill sub-kg-lifecycle: A sub-KG is a knowledge graph staged as a directory inside a harnessed repository, declared as its own layer, that may later leave for a repository of its own. The lifecycle: declare it in place, grow it, stage it for separation (one import seam, the separation guard, a self-contained rehearsal), and then, each behind an explicit owner confirmation, create the repository, copy the staged contents in with history, re-point the declaration, verify on a fresh clone and delete the in-repo copy. The light sibling of kg-separation: use this for a DATA layer that leaves whole, and kg-separation when a graph must split into a content repository and a tools repository. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . Skill id: sub-kg-lifecycle · Package: graph-management Process: sub-kg-lifecycle.bpmn Stages 6 to 13 are drawn as the phases it shares with kg-separation: authorise, move and cut over. A sub-KG created inside a folio or harnessed repository can move to its own repository later: once it is staged for separation, a new repository is created and the staged contents are copied into it.

2937.title: Which skill, this one or kg-separation?
2937.content: | the graph | use | . | holds data — an artefact index, generated pages, a library, a folio — and leaves whole | this skill | . | holds data and the code that writes it, and the two must become a content repository and a tools repository | kg-separation — its fourteen stages, the pair, FR-7 | . | is not yet a graph at all — tangled into its host | graph-detanglement first | . The two share their gates on purpose. Ready to seed? here is the same decision table, seed-readiness-gate.dmn, evaluated by the same command, and the owner’s confirmations here are the same rule, deletion-requires-confirmation. What this skill adds is the part kg-separation does not cover: a sub-KG born in the host, with no tools pair, that leaves in one piece.

2938.title: How a sub-KG is born — the intent question
2938.content: A content type’s own creation skill asks whether the new thing goes in a new repository or inside this one, and routes here for the second answer. For a folio in general that is getting-started’s add-folio branch. A harness above this one may own a creation skill for its own kind of graph; ask skill_list for it rather than improvising. In-repository is the cheaper default whenever the session is already in a harnessed repository. Every stage up to 6 is reversible with git revert, and nothing outside the repository changes until stage 7. A new repository is the first irreversible, outward-facing act, and this lifecycle puts it behind a confirmation rather than at the start.

2939.title: The stages
2939.content: Each stage names its lane (a role in scenarios/roles.json) and what decides that it is done. A stage is done when its check is green, never when the work looks finished. | # | stage | lane | done when | . | 0 | Brief, claim the work item (opening-brief) | authoring-agent | work item claimed with bun run cat beans:claim | . | 1 | Declare it in place | authoring-agent | the declaration parses; instance-repositories.test.ts green | . | 2 | Grow it in place | authoring-agent | the content type’s own gates | . | 3 | Push generic down | platform-authoring-agent | check:import-direction, check:reference-direction, check:process-bindings add nothing | . | 4 | One import seam | platform-authoring-agent | every climb out of the directory goes through <name>/platform.ts | . | 5 | Rehearse self-contained | build-pipeline | bun run cat seed:ready --layer <name> --rehearse | . | 6 | Report what would move | authoring-agent | the report is in the work item (as kg-separation stage 9) | . | 7 | Owner confirms: create the repository | administrator | an answer, recorded in the work item | . | 8 | Create the repository | administrator | it exists, empty, and was read before writing | . | — | Ready to seed? | build-pipeline | seed-readiness-gate.dmn answers settled | . | 9 | Copy the staged contents in, with history | authoring-agent | a reviewed PR on a branch of the new repository | . | 10 | Re-point the declaration | platform-authoring-agent | the host is green consuming the new repository | . | 11 | Verify on a fresh clone | build-pipeline | the new repository’s gates green from git clone in an empty directory | . | 12 | Owner confirms: delete the in-repo copy | administrator | an answer, recorded in the work item | . | 13 | Cutover commit | administrator | one commit, revertable (as kg-separation stage 13) | . 1 · Declare it in place . A directory <name>/ at the host’s root, with <name>/<name>.json: . { "name": "<name>", "repository": "<owner>/<name>", // the PLANNED home; IRIs key on it "livesAt": { "repository": "<owner>/<host>", "path": "<name>" }, // where it sits TODAY "version": "0.1.0", "needs": ["<the harness it instantiates>"], "directories": [ /* only directories that exist, each with its graphTypologies */ ] } . | repository differs from livesAt.repository — that difference is what makes the directory a staged layer, and it is what the separation guard and seed:ready read. Nothing lists the staged layers by hand. | The directory may sit anywhere — a root sibling is the convention, but the tools read livesAt.path, so folio/<name>/ works the same. | Scaffold it with init-folio --staged <path>: . bun run cat init-folio --staged <path> --title "<title>" \ --repository <owner>/<name> --needs <harness> # --host-repository when origin cannot say . It writes exactly two files, <path>/<name>.json and an empty <path>/platform.ts, and nothing at the host’s root; init-folio-staged.test.ts snapshots the whole host tree to hold that. Never --instance inside a host: it writes a repository’s worth of scaffolding (AGENTS.md, .mcp.json, a work items store, a session hook; 15 files, measured with --dry-run). --instance is for stage 8’s repository. | Declare a directory with its files, in one commit: a declared-but-absent directory is scanned as empty and reported clean. | . 3 · Push generic down — before the seam, not after . Move everything generic into the harness below, consolidate what the sub-KG needs into its own harness, and only then seed. The other order copies generic code into a repository that has to give it back. Wrong-direction edges hide in declarations and data, not only in imports: a skill definition naming a package one layer up, a dependsOn, a publication target enumerated in an input schema, prose links, a needs edge to an empty layer. So run all three direction checks, not one. 4 · One import seam: <name>/platform.ts . Every symbol the sub-KG uses from the platform is re-exported from one file, and nothing else in the directory climbs out of it. On the day it leaves, re-pointing the platform is a one-file edit instead of a sweep. cat-harness-tools/scripts/tests/instance-separation-imports.test.ts is the guard. It covers every layer whose repository differs from its livesAt.repository, not only those that opted in, because an opt-in guard is silent for exactly the layer that has no seam. Layers other layers build on are an explicit, checked exemption, and a layer that still climbs has a ceiling that may only fall. Create the seam at stage 1, not here. It costs one file on day one, and every later climb is a reroute. A merge from main is where new climbs arrive, so a red guard after one is the expected signal to reroute, not a regression. 5 · Rehearse self-contained — run the gates, do not scan . bun run cat seed:ready --layer <name> --rehearse --text # exit 0 settled, 1 not yet, 2 unknown . It copies the layer and what it needs into a scratch workspace of sibling directories and runs the tests there. It is a run rather than a reading because: . | a static import scan misses files the gates load at run time — a JSON code list read by URL, for one; | renaming the directory can change every generated page, when a URL prefix or a chrome lookup keys on the directory name. Take the identity from the declaration’s name, never from the path, and check for that before seeding into a different directory name. | . 7 and 12 · The two confirmations . Both are userTasks in the administrator lane, marked relaxable="false", and both follow deletion-requires-confirmation: the agent reports what would happen, how large it is and how it is undone, then waits. Silence is not a yes. The questions are numbered, four options at most, the recommended one first, with a stated default: . Before stage 8: . <name> is staged and rehearses green: N files, M MB, history of K commits. Creating <owner>/<name> is visible outside this repository and is not undone by a revert. May it be created? . | Yes — you create it, and tell me when it exists (recommended) | Yes — I create it (only if this session has that permission) | Not yet — keep it staged here | . Default if you do not answer: 3. Nothing is created. Before stage 13: . <owner>/<name> is green from a fresh clone and the host consumes it. The in-repo copy is N files. Deleting it is one commit, revertable. | Delete the in-repo copy now (recommended) | Keep it until the new repository’s first release | Show me the file list first | . Default if you do not answer: 2. Nothing is deleted. When the repository must be created by someone with credentials this session lacks, the hand-over is agent-handoff: one work item, one sentence for the person to relay. 9 · Copy the staged contents in, with history . The staged directory becomes the new repository’s content with its history: git subtree split --prefix=<name> in the host, then git subtree add (or a merge of the split branch) in the new repository. It goes in on a branch, as a draft PR, never straight to main. The new repository’s own root files — its declaration at the root, its config, its README — are a second commit in the same PR, so the copy itself stays byte-identical and reviewable. Ready to seed? comes first, at seed time, because the tree has moved since the rehearsal: every open PR touching the layer when the copy is taken is orphaned. Its criteria and thresholds are in kg-separation §”Ready to seed?”, and not restated here. 10 · Re-point the declaration . | what changes | how | . | livesAt | removed in the new repository — absent means “sits at the root of repository” | . | the seam | platform.ts points at wherever the platform now is: a remote-mounted path, or a sibling checkout | . | the host | remote mount if the host imports code from the sub-KG — a source.remote layer in the host’s root index.config.json (remote-mount; never a submodule); subscription (kg:subscribe) if it only reads its content | . | pins | the host pins a commit while staging, a version once released (upstream-version-adoption) | . | its site | the new repository publishes and previews itself (feature-staging, Which site): "site": { "agentRun": true } in its index.config.json when an agent publishes it, plus whatever workflow its publisher layer’s own creation skill requires (an IG’s AST-cache refresh, for one) | . | its checks | .github/workflows/harness-pr-checks.yml calling the tools layer’s layer-pr-checks.yml, so its gates run on every pull request | . | its QA record | when it declares a qa directory with storage (test/results/, cat/cat-harness/qa-reports, keyed by commit): .github/workflows/publish-qa.yml calling the tools layer’s layer-qa-publish.yml, so every push to main and every pull request publishes its results to its own qa-reports branch, and test/results/ in .gitignore. A host reads them at the commit it pins. Without the job, the declaration names a store nothing writes | . | .gitignore | the mount block, written by the mount tool between its own markers. Never typed: a hand-written marker makes remote-mount.ts refuse (markers unpaired) | . Copy these from a sibling repository of the same kind; never type them. A repository scaffolded by hand misses them, and its site cannot be built until each is copied in. The host keeps its own copy through this stage. The re-point is additive. 11 · Verify on a fresh clone . bun run cat sub-kg:verify-clone --repo <owner>/<name> --ref <seeding branch> --text # exit 0 green, 1 red, 2 unknown . The Tool sub-kg-verify-clone clones the new repository into an empty scratch directory with its submodules (and each --sibling beside it), installs, and runs its own gates script, else its test script. An empty tree, a failed clone or a repository with no gate is unknown, never green. Nothing in a seed runs standalone until the seam is re-pointed, so a test that climbs out (Cannot find module '../../../<harness>/…') fails here. A rehearsal in the host’s scratch space is not this check; it shares the host’s node_modules and network. The new repository’s own site is part of this check: bun run cat stage:local --repo . --dry-run from the fresh clone must build. A refusal names what stage 10 left out.

2940.title: Stage 13: the frozen copy
2940.content: After cutover the host keeps a frozen copy in fsh-guts, not a refreshed mirror and not a deletion. Step 12 asks (1) move to fsh-guts now, (2) keep in place until the first release, (3) show the file list first, default (2). Step 13 deposits the directory into the PARENT’s fsh-guts as a verified archive (not plain trees, which CI would audit as live content), then removes it from main. The deposit is the one state:seed --cutover makes for a state graph: an archive that must extract to the exact tree being removed, plus a provenance note (movedFrom, movedOn, sourceCommit, tree), and the removal commit is made only once it has landed. A separation targets the parent’s fsh-guts rather than the departing layer’s, which --cutover does not yet do. The live copy is the remote mount (index.config.json source.remote), npm package retrieval (kg-retrieve-npm), or subscription (kg:subscribe) from stage 10; the frozen one is never refreshed and never rendered. How checks treat a frozen subtree . This is the one place the rule is stated; scanners point here. A frozen subtree is one retired item, and its sibling note is the node that answers for it. Every reader of fsh-guts — the fsh-guts.jsonld export, the fsh-guts page, the render-pipeline and bean-reference tests, check:materialized-fixity — reports the note and does not enter the directory. The page shows it as one row in the via sidecar state. | Recognised by declaration, never by path. A directory is frozen because <name>.md beside it declares $schema: folio-fsh-guts/v1 and kind: separated-instance (isFrozenSubtree in schemas/kg/fsh-guts.ts). A copy dropped in with no note, or under a note of another kind, is walked like any directory, so its files fail self-declaration loudly rather than vanishing from every check. | The note must carry all four stage-13 fields — movedFrom, movedOn, repository, matchesCommit — because it is now the only thing any check reads about thousands of files. Those beyond the common set are exported under the node’s data. | Materialization records inside are not judged. They claim bytes in the repository the graph now lives in, which the copy deliberately does not carry. | The note’s bean: resolves against main’s work plan, with no pending escape. So the deposit lands on the fsh-guts branch in the same step that merges the PR carrying that work item, never before it; a deposit pushed ahead of its PR turns every PR’s CI red. | .

2941.title: Anti-patterns
2941.content: . | Creating the repository first. It is the one irreversible step; everything that can be done in place is done before it. | A seed with no history. A one-commit seed severs blame for every line, and the history is cheap to keep. | Re-pointing by sweep. If more than one file changes when the platform moves, the seam was skipped. | Reading the rehearsal as the fresh-clone check. They catch different things: the rehearsal catches climbs, the fresh clone catches everything the host’s environment was quietly supplying. | Deleting the in-repo copy because the new repository is green. Green is the precondition for asking, not the answer. | Committing mounted directories to the host repository. Remote mounts populate layer directories locally. If .gitignore does not ignore the mounted paths, external files pollute downstream git status. index.config.json must generate gitignore entries for all remoteMounts. | Breaking dependents when dependencies fold. If a dependency layer folds into another (e.g. cat-openapi into cat-harness), downstreams that still reference the folded layer fail unless FOLDED_INSTANCE_ALIASES maps them. | Separating before resolving withheld asset clearance. If library items are withheld or unpermitted in the separated repository (as with the IRIS replica), materialization results in broken links. Clearance must be verified at seed time. | .
