2943.title: Translation manager
2943.content: Skill translation-manager: Translation lifecycle management for folio content. Covers gettext PO/POT extraction and injection, TranslationNode manifests as KG nodes, official vs unofficial translations, staleness tracking, sign-off workflow, automatic badge rendering, the poSources fallback resolution chain, and translating into several locales as a team: one extraction, a PR per locale to main, FHIR terms as CodeSystem supplements, the untainted round trip as run, and the per-locale QA report. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . Skill id: translation-manager · Package: folio-core . Manage the translation lifecycle for folio content. This skill covers the full round trip from source content to translated content, including extraction, translation, injection, quality assurance, sign-off, and automatic badge rendering.

2944.title: Reference
2944.content: The authoritative documentation is docs/guides/translation-support.md. Read it before using this skill. This file is the operational checklist, not the architecture.

2945.title: The two-axis model
2945.content: A content node varies along two axes: . | Format — .md (Markdown), .lean (Lean 4), .tex (LaTeX), .bpmn, .dmn, etc. | Language — BCP 47 locale tags (en, fr, es, ar, zh, ru). | . The format axis is handled by companions. The language axis is handled by the PO/POT pipeline with TranslationNode manifests in translations/<locale>/.

2946.title: TranslationNode — .po/.pot files as KG nodes
2946.content: Each .po/.pot pair is wrapped by a .ts manifest that makes it a first-class node in the knowledge graph: . import type { TranslationNode } from "../../schemas/translation"; const node: TranslationNode = { label: "trans:fr/index", locale: "fr", sourceFile: "docs/index.md", potFile: "translations/fr/index.pot", poFile: "translations/fr/index.po", status: { locale: "fr", official: false, generatedBy: "agent" }, coverage: { translated: 37, total: 37, pct: 100 }, }; export default node; . The manifest carries the status, coverage, and QA results inline — no separate status.json or .qa.json files.

2947.title: PO source resolution (fallback behavior)
2947.content: Content blocks can declare explicit PO sources via poSources[] on BlockBase. When not declared, the pipeline resolves by convention: . | Block-level: translations/<locale>/<block-stem>.po | Chapter-level: translations/<locale>/<chapter-slug>.po | Folio-level: translations/<locale>/global.po | Dependency walk: walk <name>.config.json dependencies depth-first | . When poSources is declared, only the listed files are consulted (no fallback). Later entries override earlier for the same msgid.

2948.title: What is translatable
2948.content: | Content | Translatable? | Notes | . | Block titles | ✅ | From .ts manifests | . | Prose bodies (.md) | ✅ | Segmented by paragraph | . | Chapter/section titles | ✅ | From chapter.ts / section.ts | . | Kind headings | ✅ | “Definition”, “Theorem”, etc. → locale catalogue | . | LaTeX math | ❌ | Universal notation | . | Block labels | ❌ | Structural identifiers | . | Code blocks | ❌ | Programming language content | . | Lean companions | ❌ | Formal mathematics | . | FHIR resources | ⚠️ | Use FHIR’s own designation system, not gettext | .

2949.title: The exported GRAPH per locale
2949.content: The graph a machine consumes is translated per locale, not only the rendered page: bun run cat kg:locale writes it (kg:locale:bootstrap for the nested layer, kg:locale:check in the gate set). Four rules; an implementation breaks the first by default. 1. The core graph must not reference its translations. No hasTranslation, no availableLocales, no translationOf, no per-locale @id, no locale key in the @context. The obvious implementation hangs a pointer off each node; that grows the core by an edge per locale per node and makes bootstrap’s graph reference artefacts it does not own and cannot validate. The arrow runs one way — a per-locale document references the core, never the reverse — and the core is complete with no translation existing. The same relation board-diagram-interchange states for a board and its folio. localeDocumentsUnreferenced checks it rather than trusting it. 2. A translated node keeps its @id. A translation is not a new term. Locale-suffixed IRIs are ruled out by that, not chosen against. 3. The language tag rides the VALUE, never the document. A blanket "@language": "fr" would assert French over every string that fell through — and fall-through is the normal case, because parsePo takes only non-empty msgstr and skips fuzzy entries. A translated value is {"@value": …, "@language": …}; a fall-through stays a plain string under the document’s declared sourceLanguage. Fall-through is then visible in the data rather than inferable from a coverage number. 4. A catalogue is scoped to the asset it was extracted from. Merging every .po under a locale lets a docs page’s "yes" → "oui" translate every BPMN gateway branch label — output that looks right while no diagram catalogue exists, so it can only be caught by provenance, not by reading the output. So a .po is read only when its stem names an asset the graph projects. A residual is accepted and named: a msgid from diagram A applies to an identical string on a node from diagram B — not a new assumption, since kg-export already dedupes lane-derived Role nodes by lane name across every diagram. What the gate is not. kg:locale:check says nothing about how much is translated. Where a diagram template has no .po in a locale, the exporter writes nothing and reports the locale saying so. A locale with nothing to say is reported, never a missing file a reader cannot tell from a broken build; --all-locales emits a source-language copy per locale for the other reading.

2950.title: Workflow
2950.content: 1. Extract (POT generation) . bun run pipeline/pot-extract.ts [--chapter <dir>] [--block <label>] . Or use the translation_extract MCP tool. Produces .pot files at the configured granularity. 2. Build the locale term base, and review it . Before translating, build the term base for the target locale from the layered glossaries, review it, and translate with it. See The locale term base for where each layer’s glossary is and the precedence rule. The term base is the merge translation:glossary:check checks against, so build it the way that check does, not by hand from one layer. Review it before you use it: a term the more authoritative layer has fixed is not re-translated, and a term with no fixed form in any layer is a decision you make once, here, not again in every block. 3. Translate . Translate with the term base open. Options, in order of preference: . | Existing .po from SMART Base — if the DAK already has translations from Weblate/Crowdin, use them. | FHIR/translation-utils — the po-translate CLI for batch machine translation via DeepL/Google Translate. Tags results # fuzzy. | Agent translation — LLM translation of .pot → .po. Also tagged unofficial. | Human translation — the gold standard. | . Modal strength: a recommendation stays a recommendation . A lowercase should is a recommendation, and its translation is the locale’s recommendation form, never its obligation form. Turning it into “must” strengthens the claim, and in a guide it then reads as a conformance rule. Lowercase must, shall and needs to are obligations. The uppercase BCP 14 keywords (RFC 2119, RFC 8174: MUST, SHALL, SHOULD, MAY) keep the fixed renderings the locale’s term base gives them. | locale | should (recommendation) | must / shall (obligation) | . | ar | ينبغي، يُستحسن | يجب | . | es | debería, se recomienda | debe | . | fr | devrait, il est recommandé de | doit | . | ru | следует, рекомендуется | должен | . | zh | 应当, 宜, 建议 | 必须 | . A brief may not normalise one into the other, for consistency or anything else. A lexical round-trip screen cannot see this shift either: the words of a back-translation overlap whether it says “should” or “must”. So the adjudicator reads every string whose source has a modal (see “What counts as drift”). 4. Inject (PO → translated Markdown) . bun run pipeline/po-inject.ts --locale <locale> [--chapter <dir>] . Or use the translation_inject MCP tool. Reads .po files and produces translated .md in docs/<locale>/ for docs pages, or in the content directory for content blocks. 5. Create TranslationNode manifest . After injection, create or update the .ts manifest: . # The pipeline does this automatically, or create manually: translations/<locale>/<stem>.ts . The manifest carries status, coverage, and round-trip QA results inline. Validate with TranslationNodeSchema from schemas/content/translation.ts. 6. Round-trip QA . After injection, run round-trip translation QA: . bun run pipeline/translation-qa.ts --locale <locale> . Or use the translation_validate MCP tool for coverage and staleness. Semantic verification is per block and lives in the sidecar, not in a node-level summary field: TranslationNode.roundTripQA was removed with the numbers it held. See §”Per-block translation QA” below, and route drift to a human reviewer. 7. Glossary consistency . After translating, check that every glossary term was translated the way the term base fixes it, and the same way everywhere: . bun run cat translation:glossary:check --instance <dir> --locale <locale> . The check enforces a fixed term wherever the source uses it in its glossary sense; see The locale term base for how the sense is decided. It exits 1 on an in-sense use whose msgstr does not render the fixed translation. A use still pending adjudication is listed and fails nothing. To have the pending uses ruled on, list them for the adjudicator and record the answers: . bun run cat translation:glossary:check --instance <dir> --pending --json bun run cat translation:glossary:check --instance <dir> --record <verdicts.json> . Fix each violation in the .po, not in the injected output, and re-inject. Then include the check’s glossary section in the KG QA report, so the reviewer who signs off sees it. That section lists violations, exceptions, pending uses and other-sense uses. A violation the translator believes is right is not fixed by editing the term base in the layer: a term a lower layer fixes is changed in that layer, or it goes to the adjudicator. 8. Sign-off . A human reviewer signs off at the desired level: . bun run pipeline/translation-signoff.ts --locale <locale> --level <block|section|chapter|folio> [--path <content-path>] . Or use the translation_signoff MCP tool. Updates the TranslationNode manifest with sign-off metadata and source hash. 9. Staleness watch . On every content change, the pipeline checks whether any official translation’s sourceHash no longer matches the source .md. Stale translations are flagged in the viewer and in translation_status output.

2951.title: Translating into several locales as a team
2951.content: The workflow above is one catalogue’s life. When several locales are produced from the same source at the same time, by several translators, the steps are the same and the order around them matters more. The process is multi-locale-translation.bpmn, with its round trip in translation-round-trip.bpmn and its upkeep in translation-refresh.bpmn, whose steps the translation-refresh skill gives as commands. Five lanes: the owner (scope, merge window, sign-off), one source-language lead, one locale translator per locale, a back-translator and a round-trip adjudicator. Extract once, and merge the source first . The source-language lead extracts every template once: the pages, the diagrams (translate-bpmn --extract, which writes this harness’s own diagrams into its own translations/) and the glossary schemes. All of them go into one source PR to main, and it merges before any locale starts, so every translator branches from the same main. A translator never re-extracts. A locale that seems to need a different template has found a defect in the extraction, and that is reported to the lead. Each locale is its own PR to main . Each locale lands as its own PR, based on main and targeting main. Never into the source branch: a PR into an unmerged branch lands only when that branch does, and a branch that has merged and then receives more commits carries work main will never see. Once a source PR has merged, its branch receives nothing more; a later source fix is a new PR. What a locale contributes . | translations/<locale>/**.po, mirroring the templates’ layout. | A translation-node manifest beside each catalogue, official: false, generatedBy: "agent" (or "human"). No status.json: status is a property of the manifest, and officiality is a person’s sign-off, never the translator’s. | FHIR terms as CodeSystem supplements, one file per locale, holding the locale’s designations for every code system it translates. Never an edit inside a resource: an inline designation is a change to the source, every locale’s edits then collide in the same file, and the supplement is the mechanism FHIR has for exactly this. The supplements must compile with no SUSHI error and pass their structural checks (each one names the code system it supplements, at its version, and carries only codes it defines). | Source-text errors are reported, never fixed in the translation. The translator renders the source as it stands and notes the location; the lead files every such note as one issue on the source. A fix to the source is a source PR, and the next refresh carries it to every locale. | . The deterministic gates . Before any round trip, every gate passes: . | gate | command | . | templates current | translate-bpmn:check, and the layer’s page and glossary template checks | . | every catalogue matches its template | translation:drift:check --instance <root>, translation:obsolete:check --instance <root> | . | coverage | translation:status --instance <root>; a published page has its catalogue: translation:catalogue:check | . | placeholders, tags and URLs preserved | translation:page-qa --instance <root> (translation-terms-preserved) | . | officiality agrees | check:translation-officiality | . | the graph per locale | kg:locale:check | . | translated links resolve | translated-links:check | . | supplements compile | the layer’s supplement build: 0 SUSHI errors, structural checks pass | . The untainted round trip, as run . The discipline is untainted-verification and §”The agentic round trip” below; this is how it was run across several locales. | The sample, chosen by the translator before any result is seen: every diagram label, every persona and scenario string, and a seeded random fraction of the rest, with the seed recorded so the sample can be drawn again. A refresh samples only the strings it changed. | The back-translator gets the target strings alone, keyed by an opaque id, and renders them into the source language with no tools. | A mechanical pre-screen over every (source, back-translation) pair flags a pair whose negation, modal, quantifier, number or code tokens differ, and a pair whose word overlap is low. It only orders the reading. | The adjudicator reads every flagged pair in full, with the source and the back-translation and never the target, and rules each drift or not drift with its reason. | Both halves are stated. Drift: a claim added, dropped, weakened, strengthened or reversed; a term of art swapped for one that means something else; a named entity, number or quantifier moved. Not drift, and the cases that came up most: inflection; a purpose clause rendered in the subjunctive (Russian чтобы + past tense reads back as “so that … would”); an acronym left uninflected in a language that inflects nouns; an acronym spelled out with the acronym kept beside it. | Each drift is fixed on the locale’s PR, and the fix is noted beside the ruling. When two separate parties cannot be dispatched, the producer records “could not dispatch” with the reason: never a pass. | . Glossary precedence, and sense checks . The term base is layered, in this order: the normative reference glossaries first (the standards bodies’ own term lists the layer declares), then each layer in the order the index config lists it, and the layer’s own glossary last. A later layer adds terms; it never overrides a translation an earlier one fixed in the same subject area. translation:glossary:check --instance <dir> --locale <locale> checks a locale against that merge. A platform term found in text of another subject area (the harness’s policy, say, in a health guide’s prose) is a sense check for a person to read, not a violation. It fails nothing. The QA report, one per locale . Each locale’s report goes under test/results/translation-qa/: beside the per-catalogue sidecars translation:page-qa writes, a report that names coverage, each gate’s result, the round trip (sampled, flagged, drift, not drift, and every drift ruling with its fix), the glossary violations and sense checks, and the source errors reported. The lead reads it before merging the locale’s PR, inside the owner’s merge window. Harness commands for another layer’s catalogues . Every command here reads a layer through its own declaration, so one composed checkout serves every layer it mounts: . | --instance <dir> on translation:drift:check (each locale’s .po against the .pot beside it, in the layer’s translation-sources directory; a layer with no site has its catalogues compared and its pages reported unreadable), translation:obsolete:check (msgids a catalogue carries that its source no longer yields; exits 2 when the layer declares no catalogue directory), translation:index:check (the layer’s own site; exits 2 when it declares no Jekyll site) and translation:status (prints the per-locale table, writes nothing; exits 2 without a translation-sources declaration). | translation:page-qa (translation-block-qa.ts --catalogues): every <translations>/<locale>/<rel>.po with its .pot beside it, not already measured as a block or page, is measured against its template, with a sidecar at test/results/translation-qa/translations/<rel>.<locale>.translation-qa.json in the layer’s QA tree. --instance <dir> sweeps another layer. | po-inject takes its units from segmentMarkdown in pot-extract.ts, the same segmentation the extractor writes the catalogue from, so a wrapped paragraph, list item or blockquote is looked up as the one msgid it was extracted as. | translation:glossary:check is the glossary-consistency command named above. | . Exit 2 from any of them is “could not determine”, and is reported, never read as clean.

2952.title: Per-block translation QA, and the agentic round trip
2952.content: Two sweeps, two subjects, and confusing them is how a site reports a translation nobody measured. | translation-qa-sweep.ts measures the docs site: how much of each page exists in each language. It writes docs/_data/translation-qa.json and feeds the badge under a page title. | translation-block-qa.ts measures a block, one sidecar per (block, locale): <stem>.<locale>.translation-qa.json, in the block-qa/v1 entry shape, which is what the per-block TR icon opens. | . bun run cat translation:block-qa # write the sidecars bun run cat translation:block-qa:check # fail if any is stale . What a script may claim, and what it may not . Three criteria are deterministic and carry a script witness: translation-coverage, translation-terms-preserved (acronyms, numbers and URLs that must survive translation and did not — the class a fluent mistranslation passes) and translation-not-echo (a “translation” identical to its source; a warn, because that is right for a proper noun and wrong for a sentence). translation-semantic-roundtrip is written with no entry. A round trip asks whether the MEANING survived, and that needs a translator that has not seen the original. The only back-translation available to a script here is the PO’s own msgid→msgstr map read backwards, which returns the source exactly, always: a perfect similarity score measuring the lookup table. Do not fill this criterion mechanically. A green tick nobody should trust is worse than a gap that says it is a gap — a reader who sees the tick stops asking. This was not hypothetical. translations/fr/index.ts carried roundTripQA: { fail: 21, total: 36, method: "jaccard-word-overlap" }, and its own description explained those failures away as expected “with limited vocabulary back-translator” — a measurement whose author has to explain it away is about the instrument, not the translation. The generator’s back-translation map held 6 entries for 36 strings: every string nobody had back-translated scored 0 similarity and was counted as drift, so fail: 21 was a count of absences. A second script back-translated by applying a 40-pair word-substitution table to the French and wrote the result as a block-qa/v1 sidecar with an agent reviewer. All of it is removed — the numbers, the roundTripQA field, the page badge that displayed them, and both scripts. The agentic round trip — an INSTANCE of untainted verification . The discipline is generic and lives in untainted-verification: the two parties, why neither may see what would let it shortcut, the TOOLS_USED declaration that is recorded rather than assumed, which party rules, how both are written as witnesses, the model / model_source rule, and the two traps — a sweep replaces only entries whose reviewer is itself, and a verdict is hashed to what it was about. Read that first. This section is only what translation adds. The round trip was where that discipline was first written down, and generalising it turned up a defect in the generalisation: the spine’s UntaintedDispatch was typed over CompanionRole, and po is deliberately not one — a PO is a companion of a (block, locale) pair, not of a block. So the founding case could not be expressed in the type taken from it. The abstraction was widened rather than the case bent; untaintedPartitionDefects now takes its artefact universe as a parameter. The declaration . ROUNDTRIP_DISPATCH in pipeline/translation-block-qa.ts: . | party | sees | never sees | . | back-translator | po — the target text, and nothing else | md, ts | . | adjudicator | md — the original, plus the back-translation | po | . Disjoint, which is the whole rule in one line. Shown the source, a back-translator writes the source back and the check passes vacuously — measuring the lookup table rather than the translation. That is not a warning here any more: untaintedPartitionDefects reports it, and a test asserts it. What counts as drift, and what does not . Both halves, always. Told only what to look for, an adjudicator returns a style review and every translation fails. Synonyms, articles and re-ordering are not drift. A claim added, dropped, weakened, strengthened or reversed is; so is a term of art swapped for something that means a different thing, and a named entity or quantifier moved. A modal is a claim’s strength: “should” read back as “must”, or “may” as “should”, is drift, however close the words are. This is the part that does not generalise — the spine requires a drift statement and checks only that one exists, because “states what is not drift as well as what is” is a reading, and a gate pretending to measure it would be the defect the whole mechanism exists to stop. Recording it . bun run pipeline/translation-roundtrip.ts --payload <file.json> . Where it lands: translation-block-qa writes translation-semantic-roundtrip: [] on every run, and before mergeCriteria an unrelated re-run deleted a round trip a pair of agents had produced — silently, with nothing in the output to say so. That incident is why the spine carries the replace-only-your-own rule. Staleness is per locale here: the entries hash the .md, the .ts and the .po, so editing the source stales every locale’s round trip and editing one translation stales only that locale’s. The instrument, not the translation . translations/fr/index.ts carried roundTripQA: { fail: 21, total: 36, method: "jaccard-word-overlap" }, and its own description explained those failures away as expected “with limited vocabulary back-translator”. The generator’s back-translation map held 6 entries for 36 strings: every string nobody had back-translated scored 0 similarity and was counted as drift, so fail: 21 was a count of absences. A second script back-translated by applying a 40-pair word-substitution table to the French and wrote the result as a block-qa/v1 sidecar with an agent reviewer. All of it is removed — the numbers, the roundTripQA field, the page badge that displayed them, and both scripts. A measurement whose author has to explain it away is about the instrument, not the subject.

2953.title: Automatic badge rendering
2953.content: Translation badges are automatically rendered on every docs page by docs-ui.js. There is no need to manually add badge includes or front matter. How it works . | head_custom.html publishes a <script type="application/json" id="fa-translation-meta"> block on every page, reading from page front matter | docs-ui.js reads that block and auto-injects into the page title: . | 🌐 Language coverage badge — 0/5 languages (grey), 1/5 (amber), 5/5 (green) | ⚠️ Unverified warning — auto-injected when translation_status: unverified | . | . Front matter for the translation pipeline to stamp . The translation pipeline stamps this front matter on generated pages: . # Source pages (English): lang: en available_locales: ["en", "fr"] # every locale the page can be read in # Translated pages: lang: fr translation_status: unverified # or "official" translation_source: index.md # source file available_locales: ["en", "fr"] . The locale term base . A glossary term must be translated the same way on every page, and the same way in every layer that uses it. The term base is the one place that says how. Where the terms come from. Each layer’s glossary is the directory it declares with the glossary graph typology in its <instance>.json (a *.glossary.json SKOS scheme per file); a layer without that declaration has no glossary of its own and inherits its dependencies’. The terms’ translations today are the per-scheme catalogues translations/<locale>/glossary/<instance>--<scheme>.po written from those schemes, and the pins in translations/<locale>/glossary.po below. Subject areas. Owner, 2026-11-07 (glossary review, “scoped fixed terms”). Each glossary scheme declares the subject area its translations bind in, as subject (dcterms:subject, a local id such as harness-vocabulary or digital-health-trust); a term may override its scheme’s. A term with no subject, on itself or its scheme, binds only within its own scheme. Precedence applies within a subject area. The term base for a locale is the glossaries of the layer and every layer it needs, merged in layer order: within one subject area, the more authoritative (lower) layer fixes a term’s translation; a layer only adds. A layer may add a term no layer below defines, and may fix its translation. It may not give a term a lower layer has fixed, in the same subject area, a second translation; that is a violation, reported by translation:glossary:check, never an override. A term used in sense keeps its fixed translation. Owner, 2026-11-07: if a glossary term is used in the narrative in the correct context, the translated narrative uses the glossary translation. The same word is not always the same concept. The harness’s policy is fixed as 策略 (an access policy), but a health guide’s “policy” is 政策. So the sense of each use is decided by rule first, then by an agent: . | By rule. A use in a page or catalogue whose subject area is the term’s own is in sense automatically. | By an adjudicator. Any other use is pending until an untainted adjudicator agent rules on it. The agent is given the term, its skos definition and the source sentence. It rules in-sense or other-sense with a one-line reason. Alternatively it records an exception: in sense, but the fixed term is wrong here because of a reason it gives. | What the check does with each state. An in-sense use (by rule or by verdict) whose msgstr does not render the fixed translation is a violation, and the check fails. A pending use is listed and fails nothing. An other-sense use is not checked. An exception passes and is listed. | Keeping the English term. A msgstr that keeps the English term verbatim renders it only where the term is part of a code or resource name. The same term left in English in prose does not render it. | Where verdicts are kept. They are stored durably in the layer, in a committed file beside its catalogues. Each is keyed by the term’s id and a hash of the msgid. Sense is a property of the source, so one verdict serves every locale and each use is asked about once. A changed msgid invalidates its verdict, and the use is asked again. | Who decides. Each verdict names who decided it, an agent or person id, never a model. The check itself never asks a model. | . How a fixed translation is recorded. It is derived, never flagged: a term whose status is authored and whose scheme catalogue (translations/<locale>/glossary/<instance>--<scheme>.po) holds a non-empty, non-fuzzy msgstr for its prefLabel is fixed. There is no #, fixed flag and no translated label in the glossary JSON, so the catalogue stays the one place a translation lives. Whether a person has signed it off is the term’s translationStatus, per locale, official or unofficial (absent means unofficial). A pinned msgstr in glossary.po below is a QA hint, not a term base entry. The terminology glossary — translations/<locale>/glossary.po . translation-terms-preserved can see that a source term is absent from a translation. It cannot see whether that is a correct localisation or a silent loss: WHO missing from a French sentence is either OMS or a dropped term, and guessing either way is worse than saying so. The glossary is how a folio tells it which. | entry | meaning | when the term is absent | . | msgstr "OMS" | the expected form, pinned | fail — the glossary said what it should be | . | msgstr "FHIR" (identity) | must survive verbatim | fail | . | #, localised | rendered in the target language, form NOT pinned | pass | . | no entry | unknown | warn | . #, localised exists so a glossary needs no translated content. Pinning a form means authoring target-language material; the flag says the one thing the checker needs — this term gets localised, I am not pinning how — and it is reviewable by someone who reads only English. Pin a form when you want the stricter check. It is a reading rule and cannot become a mute button, which is the property to preserve if you touch it. localised only converts a would-be finding about that term into a pass: it never reaches strict tokens (a URL or a number consults no glossary — nothing localises a 3), it cannot act on a term it does not name, an entry with neither a form nor the flag is unfinished rather than permission, and each locale’s file is read alone, so marking a term in French says nothing about Arabic. Every one of those is a test in translation-block-qa.test.ts. The file is hand-authored and has no POT — schemas/content/translation.ts declares that slot, and TranslationNode.potFile is optional for exactly this. Work item he0e. available_locales includes the SOURCE language, and that is not a formality. It is the list a reader’s language bar and coverage badge are computed from — “which languages can I read this page in” — and the page is certainly readable in the one it was written in. It is not the list of translations that exist, which is what availableLocales() in pipeline/po-resolve.ts returns by resolving translations/<locale>/<stem>.po; that lookup can never name the source language, because there is no translations/en/ and there never will be. Use localesAvailableFor() in pipeline/translation-index.ts to go from one to the other. Both halves of the corpus — generated and hand-authored translated pages — must stamp the same meaning, or a badge reads a numerator larger than its denominator. Do not stamp qa_translation_* keys: stamped from a node-level round trip, they publish every string nobody back-translated as semantic drift. Per-block QA is the record: the TR icon beside each block opens <stem>.<locale>.translation-qa.json, where a verdict names the witness that reached it. docs-ui.js injects the unverified-translation warning itself, from the page’s own front matter. There is no include to add: buildLanguageBar renders the six UN languages and greys out the ones not yet translated. Do not add a translation-warning.html, language-selector.html or qa-translation-badge.html include.

2954.title: The navbar filters by locale
2954.content: Translated pages are labelled as translated content in the graph and are not shown in the navbar unless their locale is selected; with no translation, the navbar falls back to the source language. Three rules, and each is enforced somewhere different because each can break somewhere different. 1. A page is a translation because the PAGE says so . Three fields in its own front matter, and nothing else anywhere: . lang: fr # this page is French nav_exclude: true # keep it OUT of the static nav translation_source: index.md # which page it expresses . pipeline/translation-index.ts walks the site and reads those. A page with no lang is the layer’s source language — absent means the default, not unknown. Never match a directory name against a list of language subtags. A layout coincidence is not a contract, and it is wrong in both directions: a folio with a no/ chapter (Norwegian, or the English word) is silently hidden from its own navbar, and a pt-BR/ or translated-fr/ directory is silently shown as source. Neither announces itself — the navbar simply has the wrong entries in it. Put the French page at accueil-fr.md beside its source and it is indexed correctly; put an English page in a folder called fr/ and it is left alone. There is deliberately no translated-content graph typology. A declaration per locale subtree restates what every page already says and grows as O(locales × subtrees). What is translatable is a node’s content (Markdown, BPMN, …), not its schema: translatability is a property of a format within a content type. Each layer that owns a content type declares, under contentTranslations in its own <instance>.json, which formats have an extract/inject pair, and schemas/library/translation-tools.ts collects them — Markdown, LaTeX, PlantUML, SVG, ArchiMate, Excel, BPMN, FSH, FHIR JSON — and isTranslatable(contentType, extension) is the predicate. The index asks it rather than inventing a second answer, so a .json beside a page is data and never a language. translations/ is declared, as translation-sources. That one earns a kind: a .po catalogue is not content in any language, so no file inside it can declare one. There is no nav_order on a translated page. It stands where its source stands, because it replaces that item rather than joining the list. A nav_order beside a nav_exclude is two facts that contradict each other, and the check refuses it. 2. nav_exclude is the half that JavaScript cannot do . just-the-docs builds the navbar at build time, from front matter, on a static site serving the same HTML to every reader. It cannot know which locale anybody chose, so a translated page left in the nav is in it for everybody. A script can swap a nav item; it cannot un-render one without a flash of the wrong nav first. So the translations leave the static nav entirely, and a reader with no JavaScript gets the source-language navbar — the correct degraded answer rather than an arbitrary one. 3. The swap, and the fallback that is not a code path . pipeline/translation-index.ts writes docs/_data/translations.json; _includes/head_custom.html publishes it into every page as #fa-translation-index; mountNavLocale in site-chrome/assets/js/docs-ui.js reads it. With a non-source locale selected, each nav item that has a page in that locale is rewritten in place — same position, same parent, translated title, translated href, and its own dir so an Arabic item inside an English column is not laid out backwards. Fallback is the absence of a rewrite. An item with no page in the selected locale is not touched, so it keeps its source-language title and link. There is deliberately no branch for it: a fallback implemented as its own code path is a code path that can be wrong, and this one cannot be. Which locale is “selected”, in precedence order: ?lang= on the URL, then the page’s own lang when the page is a translation, then the remembered fa-locale, then the source language. A locale the index has never heard of is not honoured — labelling the navbar tlh while every item is in English is a claim the page cannot support. Three states, and the third is why the index is published as null . | data-fa-nav-index | when | what the navbar does | . | ok | the index parsed and holds pages | filter it | . | empty | it parsed and holds none | nothing to swap; every item is source language | . | unknown | no island, unparseable, or index: null because the data file was absent at build time | left exactly as built | . empty and unknown produce the same navbar and are not the same answer: one is “this folio has no translations”, the other is “this build could not tell”. A build that could not determine the translation set must never render as a folio that has none — so translation:index exits 2 rather than writing a partial index over a complete one, and the deploy fails rather than publishing it. Adding a locale . | Write the pages, each carrying lang, nav_exclude: true and translation_source. Where they sit is up to you — the convention here is <dir>/<locale>/<page>.md, and nothing depends on it. | bun run cat translation:index and commit docs/_data/translations.json. | . There is no third step and no declaration to remember. The thing that IS easy to forget is nav_exclude, which is why translation:index:check fails without it: a translated page left in the static nav is in it for every reader, whatever locale they chose, which is the bug this section records.

2955.title: Official vs unofficial
2955.content: | Attribute | Official | Unofficial | . | Human sign-off | ✅ Required | ❌ Not required | . | Viewer badge | ✅ Green | 🔄 Grey/amber | . | Source hash tracking | ✅ Yes | ❌ No | . | Staleness detection | ✅ Yes | N/A | . | Can be shown in viewer | Always | Configurable (officialRequired in config) | .

2956.title: Six UN languages
2956.content: The default supportedLocales in the layer’s config (its index.config.json entry): . | Code | Language | Native | . | ar | Arabic | العربية | . | zh | Chinese | 中文 | . | en | English | English | . | fr | French | Français | . | ru | Russian | Русский | . | es | Spanish | Español | . Folios may add or remove locales. The viewer reads the list from config.

2957.title: translations/ directory rules
2957.content: The translations/ directory contains only three file types: . | .pot — POT templates (extractable strings) | .po — PO translated strings | .ts — TranslationNode manifests (KG nodes) | . Do not put .md, .qa.json, or status.json files in translations/. Rendered output lives in docs/<locale>/; QA and status are properties of the TranslationNode manifest. A layer with no translations directory of its own is hosted. translationsHomeFor (schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts) puts its templates in the extracting harness’s translations/<locale>/<stub>/ — cat-harness/translations/<locale>/bootstrap/processes/*.pot for bootstrap’s three diagrams — rather than inside the layer, which holds no translation machinery. The templates are extracted from the bootstrap the harness has pinned; when bootstrap is its own repository they stay here, since a template is the harness’s work over bootstrap’s text, not part of it (kg-separation §”The pair”).

2958.title: A layer that defines its own translator
2958.content: A layer built on this one may define its own translator actor and translation subsystem. Then the rule is load it; never vendor it: the subsystem is invoked from that layer’s checkout, not copied here, and that layer’s skills say how. This skill names no layer above it.

2959.title: IG Publisher i18n
2959.content: For FHIR IG folios, the IG Publisher’s own i18n system is used in parallel: . | i18n-default-lang in sushi-config.yaml — source language. | i18n-lang — target languages. | translation-sources — path to input/translations/{lang}/ containing per-resource .po files. | Run with -generation-off -validation-off flags for fast translation-only builds. | . The prose translation pipeline (this skill) and the FHIR resource translation pipeline (IG Publisher) are complementary and independent.

2960.title: Do not
2960.content: . | Do not manually add badge includes. docs-ui.js renders them automatically from front matter. The include it replaced is deleted, not deprecated — an include that still exists is one somebody adds back. | Do not publish a semantic-QA number a script cannot establish. A back-translation from this repo’s own PO map, or from a word-substitution table, scores the table rather than the translation — and a string with no back-translation at all scores 0 and reads as drift. If no independent back-translator has run, the criterion has no verdict, and saying so is the honest output. | Do not infer a locale from a directory name. docs/fr/index.md is French because it says lang: fr. A subtag match is wrong in both directions and neither failure announces itself — see The navbar filters by locale. | Do not add a graph typology for translated content. It is the same kind of thing as the page it translates, differing by a field the file declares. Translatability is a property of a FORMAT within a content type — schemas/library/translation-tools.ts and isTranslatable — not of a directory. | Do not leave a translated page in the static nav. nav_exclude: true is what keeps it out, and no amount of client-side work substitutes for it: the nav is built once, for every reader, before anybody has chosen a locale. | Do not put non-PO files in translations/. Only .pot, .po, and .ts manifests belong there. Rendered .md goes in docs/<locale>/. | Do not vendor SMART Base translation scripts. Load from checkout. | Do not translate math, labels, or code. Exclude in extraction. | Do not auto-sign-off. Official status requires a human. | Do not re-extract per locale. Templates are extracted once, merged to main in one source PR, and every locale starts from them. | Do not open a locale PR into the source branch, and do not push to a branch whose PR has merged. Each locale is its own PR to main. | Do not fix the source in a translation. Report it as one issue. | Do not edit a FHIR resource to translate it. Its terms go into the locale’s CodeSystem supplement. | Do not re-translate a term a lower layer fixes in the same subject area. Translate with the locale term base, and fix a violation where the term is fixed. A use in another subject area is enforced once an adjudicator rules it in sense; until then it is pending, not a violation. | Do not treat staleness as “wrong”. A stale translation is still useful; it just needs re-review. | Do not conflate FHIR resource translation with prose translation. They are different pipelines with different tooling. | Do not auto-remove staging previews. Require staging:cleanup label. | .

2961.title: Content-type-specific translation tools
2961.content: Each content type declares what formats it can translate and what scripts handle each format. The declaration belongs to the layer that OWNS the content type, under contentTranslations in its <instance>.json; schemas/library/translation-tools.ts collects every present layer’s profiles and refuses a content type declared twice. A module or diagram path in a profile resolves from the declaring layer, then down its needs chain. The profiles: . | Content type | Formats | RTL | . | document | Markdown | ✅ | . | paper | Markdown + LaTeX | — | . | dak (WHO L2) | Markdown + PlantUML + SVG + ArchiMate + Excel + BPMN | ✅ | . | ig (WHO L3) | Markdown + FSH + FHIR JSON | ✅ | . The generic pipeline (pot-extract.ts, po-inject.ts) handles Markdown. Adapter-specific tools extend it with format-specific extractors. The Python originals from SMART Base live in scripts/translation/ and are referenced in the registry. RTL support . Arabic (and Hebrew, Farsi, Urdu) pages are detected at load time by docs-ui.js and get dir="rtl" on <html>. The CSS in docs-ui.css provides smooth 0.4s transitions for sidebar and content layout: . | Sidebar slides to the right side | Content flows RTL | Mermaid diagrams and badges stay LTR | BPMN diagrams need re-rendering with translated labels | . Staging review . When presenting translated content for review, use the staging-review skill to provide before/after URL comparison tables. See schemas/sdlc/staging.ts for the StagingComparison schema.

2962.title: Staging links
2962.content: When a staging preview exists, every request this skill makes for feedback, review or sign-off carries it: one deep link per changed page, to the anchor where the change sits, with the same page on main as before. Where the skill declares an output contract, they go in its stagingLinks field. The rule, and where the page list comes from: feedback-deep-links.

2964.title: Adopting an upstream version bump
2964.content: Skill upstream-version-adoption: Watch a pinned upstream dependency for a new release, and take a candidate version through impact analysis, an MVP build, review and a person’s adopt/hold/decline decision. Reusable per pin — the theme is the first tenant, not the only one. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . An unpinned dependency is an unreviewed commit from a stranger, merged on every build. A pinned one is a commitment that somebody has to revisit. This skill is the second half: what happens between upstream cut a release and we are running it. It implements two diagrams, and the diagram is the source of truth for ordering: . | Diagram | What it is | . | upstream-pin-watch.bpmn (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) | The watcher. Scheduled, mechanical, ends at either “every pin is current” or “one tracking issue says which is not”. | . | upstream-version-adoption.bpmn (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) | The reusable subprocess, entered once per stale pin. Scope → impact → MVP → review → decide. | . The second is called, not copied: calledElement="Process_UpstreamAdoption". Any pinned upstream dependency enters it the same way, and a new tenant is a registry row plus a call activity — never a second diagram that says the same thing in different words.

2965.title: The registry is the tenant list, and it does not hold the version
2965.content: upstream/upstream-pins.json — in this harness’s declared upstream/ directory — declares each pinned dependency, with each pinnedIn resolved against the harness root: the upstream repo, the file the pin literal actually lives in, the pattern that reads it, what of ours binds to it, and the commands that constitute its MVP. It deliberately does not store the pinned version. The version lives in exactly one place — site-chrome/_config.yml for the theme — and the registry says how to read it from there. A registry that carried its own copy would be a second answer to “what are we running”, free to disagree with the build. bun run cat check:upstream-pins reads the literal out of the declared file; a pattern that matches nothing is reported as an error, not as “no pin”. binds and mvp are the reason the registry exists at all rather than the check simply grepping for version strings. They are what turn impact analysis and MVP from words in a box into a list somebody can work through.

2966.title: 1 — Watch
2966.content: bun run cat check:upstream-pins, weekly from .github/workflows/upstream-pins.yml and on demand. For each row: read the pinned ref out of its declared file, list the upstream tags that match tagPattern, and compare. Exit codes, and the middle one is the point: . | Exit | Meaning | What the workflow does | . | 0 | every pin is at the newest matching release | closes the tracking issue if one is open | . | 1 | at least one pin is behind | opens one issue labelled upstream-pin, or edits the existing one | . | 2 | could not determine — upstream unreachable, pattern did not match | leaves the issue untouched and fails the job | . Three rules it inherits from check-ci-health.ts, and they are not optional: . | “Could not check” is never rendered as current. An unreachable upstream is exit 2, not exit 0. A watchdog that goes blind must not read as good news. | One issue, edited in place. An edit does not notify, so a pin that stays stale for months stays one unread item rather than many. | The job fails on exit 2, which makes this workflow itself red on the default branch, which check:ci-health reports. The watchdog is watched. | .

2967.title: 2 — Impact analysis
2967.content: Scope the delta first, and scope it to what reaches our output. The upstream changelog is the claim; the diff is the evidence. For a Jekyll theme that means _sass, _includes, _layouts and assets — a change to upstream’s own docs, CI or tests cannot reach us: . git -C <upstream-clone> diff --stat <pinned>..<candidate> -- _sass _includes _layouts assets . Then ask what of ours binds to it, from the row’s binds list. This is the half that a changelog cannot tell you, because upstream does not know what you reached into. For the theme it is concrete and small: site-chrome/assets/js/docs-ui.js moves the theme’s own search markup into the action launcher, binding .search, #search-input and .search-label; site-chrome/assets/css/docs-ui.css overrides .side-bar, .site-header and .main-header; and three e2e specs assert the structure the theme emits. An upstream rename of any of those is not a build failure — it is a shipped feature that quietly stops working, which is the failure mode a pin exists to convert into a decision. Write the analysis down as the work item’s note before building anything. A candidate that touches nothing we bind to is a different conversation from one that renames a selector we depend on, and the reviewer needs to know which they are looking at before they look.

2968.title: 3 — MVP
2968.content: An MVP is a deployed build, not a description of one. Move the pin on a branch, let feature-staging.yml publish it under branches/<branch-slug>/, and run the row’s mvp commands. For the theme: . rm -rf _kg _site bun test # unit tests CI=1 bun run cat test:e2e # a11y, action tiles, sidebar panels, qa panel bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/site-links.ts --site ./_site # every navbar tile resolves in the BUILT site . site-links.ts checks the tiles against the real _site rather than against the attribute, which is what catches a tile that 404s. A red gate is evidence, not an exit. It does not end the process and it does not loop on its own — it goes to the reviewer with everything else, because “this version breaks us” is a finding the decider needs, not a reason to stop before they see it.

2969.title: 4 — Review
2969.content: Post the staging URL, the gate results and the impact analysis on the PR, then hand it over. The reviewer’s question is narrower than “is the new version good”: it is does anything in binds still hold, checked against the deployed page rather than against a screenshot. Findings the agent can fix — our overlay adapting to a renamed class, a test fixture updated to the markup the theme now emits — loop back into impact analysis on the same branch. Findings that are upstream’s behaviour rather than ours go to the decision as they are.

2970.title: 5 — Decide
2970.content: A person decides, and the diagram says so. PM_Decide is a bpmn:userTask in the publication manager’s lane, and that role admits person only, so activity-fulfilment-kind fails the moment somebody tries to make an agent the accepting party. It also carries <cat-harness.processes:policy relaxable="false"/>: no package may relax it. The lane is the publication manager’s rather than the editor’s because the pin is not a change to the corpus — it is a change to what the published artefact is built from, and that role is the one “accountable for what is live”. The gateway is not DMN-backed, and that is deliberate. Every other computed gateway in this repository reduces to arithmetic over tool output; this one weighs a rendering nobody can score against the cost of staying behind. A table here would look authoritative and would not be. Three outcomes: . | Adopt — move the pin, open the PR, and say in the body what the version range changed in rendered output. Record the evidence you used, not just the verdict. | Hold — record it as a block with an expiry and a revisit trigger (bean-blocking.md (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan)). A hold with no expiry cannot be told from abandoned work, and the next watcher run will re-raise the same pin with no memory of why it was left. | Decline — record the reasons on the work item and scrap it. A scrapped work item is what stops the next agent re-entering the same dead end; a deleted one leaves them unable to tell a decision from an accident. | . In every case the decision is written down before the process ends. The work item is resolved from the terminal step, so a run that stops at “we looked and said no” is as finished as one that moved the pin.

2971.title: Adding a tenant
2971.content: . | Pin the literal wherever the tool reads it, with a comment saying which process governs moving it. | Add a row to upstream-pins.json: repo, pinnedIn, pattern, tagPattern, binds, mvp. | Run bun run cat check:upstream-pins and confirm it reads your pin back. A pattern that does not match is exit 2 — “could not determine” — and the row is not watched until it does. | . No diagram changes. That is what reusable means here.

2972.title: How to pick the pinned version when you first pin something
2972.content: Pin what is running, not what is newest. Those are different changes, and doing both at once means neither is reviewable — a regression cannot be attributed to the pin or to the bump. Establish what is running by fingerprint, not by assumption. For the theme that meant finding a declaration in the deployed CSS on gh-pages (text-wrap: balance, in _sass/navigation.scss) that entered upstream after the newest release, which proved the live site was tracking the default branch rather than any tag. The newest release at or below that point is the pin, and the PR states the residual delta — one CSS declaration — rather than claiming there is none. If no fingerprint discriminates, say so and pin the newest release anyway; an unverified pin is still strictly better than an unpinned dependency, and “could not determine” written down is worth more than a confident guess.
